source: Magnetic Flux
Φ = BA cos θ counts the field passing through a loop, with θ measured from the loop's normal.
Students measure the angle from the loop's plane instead of its normal.

Faraday's discovery, coming up next, depends on one quantity: how much magnetic field passes through a loop of wire. That amount is the magnetic flux. It uses the cosine from Sine, Cosine and Tangent and the field you met in Magnetic Fields and Their Sources.

For a flat loop of area $A$ in a uniform field $B$, $$\Phi = BA\cos\theta,$$ where $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{B}$ and the loop's normal (the line sticking straight out of the loop). The unit is the weber: $1\ \text{Wb} = 1\ \text{T·m}^2$.

Think of field lines as rain and the loop as a hoop. Held flat under the rain, the hoop catches the most. Tilted, it catches less, because the area it shows to the rain shrinks to $A\cos\theta$. Held edge-on, it catches none. The flux counts field lines the same way: $B$ times the area facing the field.
Tilt the loop. The flux is largest at $\theta = 0$, when the field passes straight through, and zero at $90^\circ$, when the loop lies along the field.

Measuring $\theta$ from the plane of the loop instead of from its normal. If a problem says "the field makes $30^\circ$ with the plane of the loop", the angle from the normal is $90^\circ - 30^\circ = 60^\circ$. Quick check: a field lying in the loop's plane must give zero flux, and $\cos 90^\circ = 0$ does that.
A loop of area $0.050\ \text{m}^2$ sits in a $0.40\ \text{T}$ field. Its normal is $60^\circ$ from the field. Find the flux.
A tilted loop
$$\Phi = BA\cos\theta = (0.40)(0.050)\cos 60^\circ.$$
$\cos 60^\circ = 0.50$, so $\Phi = 0.010\ \text{Wb}$.
A circular loop of radius $0.10\ \text{m}$ is in a $0.20\ \text{T}$ field that makes $30^\circ$ with the plane of the loop. Find the flux.
Angle from the plane
Angle from the normal: $\theta = 90^\circ - 30^\circ = 60^\circ$.
A coil of $N$ turns has the same flux through each turn, so the total, $N\Phi$, is $N$ times bigger. You will use that in Faraday's law.
